Deux immigrantes intégrées sont forcées: Two well-integrated immigrant women are forced to leave Quebec because of more restrictive immigration policies.
Magaly Cornejo a quitté le Canada à la m: Magaly Cornejo left Canada in mid-October after her work permit was not renewed. Photo credit: Maria Gabriela Aguzzi
Pendant l’été, alors que je faisais un r: This summer, while I was reporting from a francization centre in LaSalle, someone I was interviewing told me about Magaly Cornejo: a Mexican woman of admirable strength who showed up to class all smiles and ready to learn French… after working all night in an airport restaurant.
J’ai tout de suite voulu la rencontrer,: I immediately wanted to meet her, write her portrait, understand her routine and what motivated her to make such a sacrifice. But by the time I finally reached her, her story had just taken a sharp turn: because of the changes to Quebec’s immigration rules, her work permit had not been renewed.
Je lui ai demandé si elle voulait rester: I asked her if she wanted to stay in Quebec, and she answered with a “yes” weighed down by deep frustration. I figured there had to be other people in the same situation, people from diverse backgrounds living all over the province. I put out a call on social media, and a colleague put me in touch with María Caballero, an artist who came here fleeing the war in Ukraine with her husband. Speaking with her confirmed that the closing of doors affects a wide range of profiles, in a province caught between political pressures and very real economic needs.
Pour mieux comprendre les répercussions: To better understand the human toll of the Quebec government’s immigration measures and to go beyond individual accounts, I also spoke with sociologist Alejandro Hernández, a professor at Concordia University.
Pendant deux ans, l’aéroport Pierre-Elli: For two years, Montréal’s Pierre-Elliott-Trudeau airport was where Magaly Cornejo wove her hope, washing floors, making pizzas and serving coffee in the middle of the night while the city slept. Ironically, that same airport became her way out. This Mexican woman did not leave by choice, but because her profile no longer “fit” the Quebec government’s immigration needs.
Son histoire recoupe celle de María Caba: Her story intersects with that of María Caballero, a French-Spanish artist who fled Kyiv with her Ukrainian husband and arrived in Montréal intending to rebuild her life. Almost three years later, she has discovered that her “host land” has turned into an impassable bureaucratic wall.
Ces deux femmes représentent les extrême: These two women represent the extremes of the temporary migration spectrum: on one side, a low-wage essential worker; on the other, a francophone artist with international experience. But they share the same fate and the same feeling: the frustration of being pushed out by an immigration system that seems to be growing ever more restrictive.
Magaly est arrivée au Québec avec un per: Magaly arrived in Quebec with a temporary work permit. Originally from Veracruz, she was looking for opportunities that had been denied to her in Mexico because of her age. Firm in character, always smiling and with a contagious optimism, she dreamed of staying in Montréal despite her longing for her “México lindo y querido.”
« Mon pays est magnifique, mais après 45: “My country is beautiful, but after 45, the doors close,” she laments.
Avant de s’établir avec un statut de tra: Before settling in with temporary worker status, she had spent six months in Montréal as a tourist – long enough to start the paperwork, go back to Mexico and wait for approval from the Canadian government. A job was waiting for her at an airport restaurant open 24 hours a day. She had started out cleaning and helping in the kitchen, but her dedication quickly earned her other tasks, like making pizzas, brewing coffee and serving customers.
Son horaire – de 22 h à 6 h – était un d: Her schedule – 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. – was a challenge few people can accept. Even so, Magaly had decided to keep moving forward and had signed up for French classes. Her routine was gruelling: after her night shift, she would go home, shower, eat a little and head back out to her francization centre in LaSalle, where she studied until noon. She slept barely two or three hours. “By 6 p.m., I was already up, full of energy,” she says, laughing.
En raison de ce rythme soutenu, elle s’e: The relentless pace left her with a back injury, but she was able to receive medical care and physiotherapy. She also had the support of her boss, Mohamed, who recognizes “the work ethic of Latinos.” But neither her efforts nor her integration were enough, because her work permit was not renewed. Her profile is among those hit by the cuts Quebec imposed on low-wage temporary workers in September 2024.
Magaly est frustrée, mais reconnaissante: Magaly is frustrated, but grateful to have a home to return to. What worries her is how hard it will be to re-enter the Mexican job market and the wages waiting for her there. She still holds on to a glimmer of hope, though, as she is considering learning a trade to try her luck again, perhaps in Alberta. “It’s better to come back and go in legally,” she says.
Le cas de Magaly n’est pas isolé. Selon: Magaly’s case is not isolated. According to Alejandro Hernández, a sociologist and professor at Concordia University, Quebec’s political decisions are part of a historical ideology marked by a sense of identity vulnerability. Within that framework, the CAQ government has consolidated a discourse focused on “protecting” and building a nation perceived as under threat.
« Un des axes centraux de ces changement: “One of the central axes of these immigration changes responds to what politicians present as the cornerstone of identity,” Hernández explains. In this discourse, immigrants, especially those who don’t fit the ideal of the white francophone, are seen as an “other,” a potential consumer of public resources, he adds.
Cette idéologie contraste pourtant avec: This ideology contrasts sharply with economic reality, however. Employers have been saying for years that they can’t recruit enough employees for essential positions, particularly night shifts, manufacturing, services and agriculture.
Malgré cela, le gouvernement de François: Despite this, François Legault’s government has announced a gradual reduction in permanent residency thresholds: from about 60,000 new residents this year to about 45,000 in 2026. Immigration Minister Jean-François Roberge justifies the measure by citing pressure on public services, the situation at the southern border and certain federal government decisions.
Depuis septembre 2024, les employeurs ne: Since September 2024, employers can no longer hire more than 10% of their workforce through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) under its low-wage stream (for staff paid less than $32.96 an hour), unless they are trying to address labour shortages in the health care, construction and food manufacturing sectors – where the 20% cap remains in place.
Pour des milliers de travailleurs comme: For thousands of workers like Magaly, this rule shut the door on Quebec without warning.
Penser que ces politiques touchent seule: It would be a mistake to think these policies only affect unskilled workers. The cuts have made the system so rigid that it is pushing out even the talent the province says it wants to attract. While Magaly was pushed aside as a low-wage temporary worker, María Caballero discovered that neither her native French, nor her training, nor her artistic experience was enough.
Danseuse et chorégraphe menant une carri: A dancer and choreographer with an international career, she arrived in Montréal in August 2022 with her Ukrainian husband through the CUAET program, which gave her an open work permit for three years. Her partner quickly integrated into the job market. She did not.
Malgré sa maîtrise du français, de l’ang: Despite being fluent in French, English and Spanish, landing a stable job was almost impossible. She sent out countless résumés, to no avail. She tried to continue her career in the arts, teaching flamenco classes, but the cultural scene offered her no stability.
« Je ne sais plus combien de courriels j: “I don’t know how many emails I’ve sent anymore… I looked for work everywhere… It makes me laugh when people say, ‘Oh, you speak French, you’re not going to have any problem in Montréal.’ Well, I find it’s not that simple. I speak French, English, all the languages you need in Canada, but I had a hard time and I found nothing,” she says.
La goutte qui a fait déborder le vase n’: The straw that broke the camel’s back was not the lack of work – her husband, an animated film director, has integrated well into the job market – but the announcement that temporary residents would no longer have access to permanent residency. “Quebec no longer grants permanent residency to temporary residents. That’s what made us understand we had to leave,” María explains.
Après presque trois ans d’efforts, le co: After almost three years of effort, the couple realized Montréal would not allow them to build a future. “We stayed almost three years in Montréal for nothing… All we did was of no use to us,” she laments.
Suivant les conseils d’avocats, ils ont: Following the advice of lawyers, they moved to Halifax, Nova Scotia. There, María quickly found a job as a French and English professor at Université Sainte-Anne. Her French was immediately seen as an asset.
La stabilité a toutefois un prix, car el: Stability comes at a price, though, as she now has to accumulate a full year of experience in order to apply for permanent residency through the provincial program. To get there, she sometimes works up to 12 hours a day – even experiencing a degree of burnout.
La désillusion est profonde. « Pour moi,: The disillusionment runs deep. “For me, Canada is hard. People are hard. In Montréal, people aren’t nice. It’s very hard.”
Les histoires de Magaly et de María mett: The stories of Magaly and María highlight the human and psychological cost of immigration policies, says Alejandro Hernández, who acknowledges that this dimension of the issue is almost absent from the political debate.
« Je pense que, dans les situations qu’o: “I think that in the situations we’re living through right now, the human being takes a back seat, especially because people are directly affected: job losses, rents that are too high and keep climbing, growing insecurity… The whole question of homelessness, violence, mental health problems is there. It seems like almost everywhere, people are starting to see these situations,” adds the sociologist.
Mais pour ce qui est des immigrants, il: But when it comes to immigrants, it’s worth remembering that many sold their homes, fled conflicts or invested their savings in a life project, only to find themselves trapped in a system that changes the rules without warning.
Les justifications officielles – la cris: The official justifications – the housing crisis, pressure on health care – hold up poorly against research showing that immigrants often arrive in better health than the local population (<l1>Study on hospitalization rates</l1>, Statistics Canada) and that the housing crisis is linked to many factors, not only immigration, Hernández adds.
Pendant que le gouvernement du Québec se: While the Quebec government debates how far to open or close its doors, thousands of people remain in limbo – a reminder that immigration policy is not only about numbers, but a mirror of society.
